title: Bengaluru Couple Quits IT Jobs, Builds Rs 56 Lakh Meal Startup Serving 55,000 Meals
excerpt: Diya Krishnakumar and Adithya Natarajan launched Wellfed in September 2024 with Rs 15 lakh. Nine months of 2026 alone brought Rs 56 lakh in revenue.
body:
• Bengaluru couple Diya Krishnakumar and Adithya Natarajan quit IT jobs and launched Wellfed, a healthy meal subscription startup, in September 2024 with Rs 15 lakh from their savings.
  • Wellfed earned Rs 56 lakh between January and September 2026 — more than its roughly Rs 45 lakh in its first year — and has delivered more than 55,000 meals to over 1,500 customers, the founders told Startup Pedia.
  • The menu is home-style Indian food — dal, aloo gobhi, jowar roti, adraki chicken and chole chaat — built around protein sources such as paneer, tofu, soya and chicken.
  • Subscriptions are priced per meal: Rs 289 for a three-day trial, Rs 279 on a two-week plan and Rs 269 on a monthly plan.

For Diya Krishnakumar and Adithya Natarajan, the business idea was their own dinner problem. Working in IT in Bengaluru, they often came home too tired to cook, ordered takeaway instead, and could not find a meal subscription that served simple, healthy Indian food at a price they considered affordable. In September 2024, they quit their IT careers and built the service themselves.

Both founders studied computer science in Bengaluru and began their careers at the same IT company, spending more than three years in the sector before pursuing an MBA, according to profiles by Startup Pedia and BestVantage Investments. Neither came from the food or hospitality industry.

"A 20-minute recipe online takes twice as long when you start making it in your kitchen. Expecting that out of someone who has just spent the entire day in a cubicle, often in a high-pressure environment, is kind of a big ask."

— Diya Krishnakumar, co-founder, Wellfed, to Startup Pedia

Rs 15 lakh, six people, one dabba idea

Wellfed launched in September 2024 with an initial investment of Rs 15 lakh, largely from the couple's personal savings. The first team had six people, including the founders, a nutritionist, a cook, a steward and a delivery person. The nutritionist helped design the meals and their nutritional composition; the founders first sent meals to friends and family to test the response.

The menu deliberately avoids elaborate restaurant dishes. Alongside dal, aloo gobhi, jowar roti, adraki chicken and chole chaat, it includes wraps, biryanis and Indo-Chinese dishes, using protein sources such as paneer, tofu, soya and chicken. Meals arrive in reusable lunch containers with steel lining, sourced from a manufacturer in Maharashtra — packaging the founders designed to feel like a home dabba rather than a disposable delivery box. An early collaboration, a reel shared by a Bengaluru-based nutritionist, helped Wellfed reach its first 100 customers.

The numbers: Rs 45 lakh, then Rs 56 lakh in nine months

In its first year of operations, Wellfed generated approximately Rs 45 lakh in revenue. Between January and September 2026 it recorded Rs 56 lakh — surpassing the full first year in nine months. In total, the startup has delivered more than 55,000 meals to over 1,500 customers.

The subscription pricing explains the repeat-purchase model: a three-day trial costs Rs 289 per meal, a two-week plan Rs 279 per meal and a monthly plan Rs 269 per meal. The subscriptions include lunch and dinner, free delivery and nutritionist guidance, with meal carry-forwards available on the longer plans, according to Startup Pedia.

Not a smooth run

In early 2026, LPG shortages disrupted Wellfed's kitchen operations and forced the founders to modify the menu, slowing growth in that period. Hiring, kitchen operations and delivery logistics were early challenges as well, the founders have said.

What the founders want next

Diya and Adithya say the next step is to widen delivery coverage across Bengaluru, increase kitchen capacity and reach customers beyond the city's IT and startup hubs. They are also exploring additional dietary options and protein-rich additions, and are considering Hyderabad as a next market. Whether a single-city, home-style meal subscription can scale without losing the consistency that built it is the open question — for now, the model that solved the founders' own dinner problem is serving more than 55,000 meals and counting.
